title: How to Isolate Bass & Vocals with Demucs AI
description: Learn how to split audio stems and isolate bass, vocals, and drums using the state-of-the-art Demucs AI models for free in your browser.
author: Abhinav Vaidya
html:
Whether you want to create a high-quality karaoke backing track, isolate a bassline to transcribe it, or sample a clean vocal acapella, stem separation AI has revolutionized music production.

At the center of this revolution is Demucs — a deep learning model developed by Meta AI Research that splits audio files into distinct tracks. In this comprehensive guide, we'll show you how to use Demucs for free in your browser, explain the technology behind it, and show you exactly how musicians, producers, and content creators are using stem separation in their daily workflow.

What is Demucs?

Demucs stands for Deep Extractor for Music Sources. Unlike traditional EQ-based filters (which cut highs and lows and leave muddy artifacts), Demucs uses a convolutional neural network (CNN) / transformer architecture trained on thousands of multitrack recordings to reconstruct separate channels from scratch.

The key insight of Demucs is that it doesn't just apply a filter — it reconstructs each stem from the ground up using a learned understanding of what a vocal, a drum kit, a bass guitar, and a piano actually sound like. This produces dramatically cleaner results than older methods like FastICA or REPET that relied purely on signal processing.

It can split a stereo track into up to 6 stems:

  1. Vocals (Clean acapella)
  2. Drums (Isolated percussion including hi-hats, snare, kick)
  3. Bass (Low-end bass guitar, synth bass, or 808)
  4. Guitar (Electric and acoustic guitars)
  5. Piano (Acoustic and electric pianos, Rhodes, organ)
  6. Other (Synthesizers, brass, strings, and effects)

A Brief History of Stem Separation Technology

Understanding how far the technology has come puts the current quality in perspective.

Pre-2010: Stem separation was only possible with the original multitrack recordings from the studio. If you did not have the original session files from the recording engineer, you could not separate the stems. This made remixing and sampling a legal and technical minefield.

2010-2015: The first signal-processing approaches emerged, primarily using Robust PCA and Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF). These produced very rough separations with heavy artifacts — audible "ghost" sounds and pitch distortion.

2018: The Spleeter Era (Deezer): Deezer Research released Spleeter, a convolutional U-Net model that for the first time produced commercially usable vocal separations. Spleeter became the backbone of many apps and was a quantum leap in quality, though it still struggled with dense mixes.

2022: Demucs v4 (Meta AI Research): Meta released Demucs v4 (also called HTDemucs — Hybrid Transformer Demucs), combining convolutional processing in both the time domain and frequency domain with a cross-domain transformer layer. This produced the best-in-class results for all stem types, particularly bass and drums which previous models struggled with.

This is the model powering the Guitariz Stem Separator today.

How to Use Demucs Free Online

To run Demucs on a local computer, you usually need a powerful GPU, Python familiarity, and command-line knowledge. We have deployed Demucs models directly to the web so any musician can use it without any setup.

Here is how to split your first track using the Guitariz Stem Separator:

Step 1: Upload Your Audio File

Drag and drop any MP3, WAV, or FLAC file into the extractor box. To ensure optimal results, try to use high-quality audio files (320kbps MP3 or lossless WAV). Low-bitrate files (128kbps MP3) have pre-existing compression artifacts that reduce separation quality.

Step 2: Choose Your Stem Model

  • If you just want an acapella or karaoke track, use the Vocal Splitter (2-Stem). It splits the audio into pure Vocals and a combined Instrumental backing track. The 2-stem model is faster and often produces slightly cleaner results for vocal-only separation because it focuses the neural network's capacity on a single separation task.
  • If you want individual instruments (like isolating just the bass or piano), use the Stem Separator (6-Stem). This runs the full Demucs 6-source model and returns each instrument as an individual WAV file.

Step 3: Process and Mix

Click the Separate button. The server will run the Demucs pipeline and return the individual tracks. You can use the built-in browser mixer to mute, solo, and adjust the volume of each instrument in real-time — even before downloading anything.

Step 4: Download Stems

Once you are happy with the mix, download the individual stems as high-quality WAV files for import into your DAW (like Ableton, FL Studio, or Logic Pro).

Real-World Use Cases

For Guitarists: Transcribing Bass Lines

Bass transcription is one of the most challenging skills in ear training because the low frequencies are hard to isolate against a full band mix. With stem separation:

  1. Upload the song to the Stem Separator
  2. Download just the isolated bass stem
  3. Import the bass-only WAV into your DAW or audio player
  4. Slow it down using Audacity's "Change Tempo" (no pitch shift)
  5. Transcribe every note from the now-clear, isolated bass track

The difference in transcription speed is dramatic. A bass line that would take an hour to work out by ear from a full mix can often be transcribed in 10-15 minutes from a clean isolated stem.

For Vocalists: Karaoke & Acapella Practice

Creating karaoke backing tracks: Use the Vocal Splitter to remove the lead vocal. The remaining instrumental is a perfect karaoke backing track at the exact tempo and key of the original song — no need to search for low-quality karaoke versions online.

Acapella extraction for pitch practice: Extract just the vocal stem. Use it alongside a pitch-correction tool or simply as a reference to study the exact vocal inflections, vibrato, and pitch ornaments of your favourite singers.

For Producers: Sampling and Remixing

With isolated stems, you can:

  • Sample a hook without the background noise. Extract just the vocal chorus or guitar riff you want.
  • Create stems for remixes. Licensed remixers and bootleg producers both use stem separation to build new arrangements from existing songs.
  • Analyse mixing techniques. Listen to the kick drum in isolation to understand how it was tuned and EQ'd. Listen to the dry vocal to understand the mic and recording chain. These insights are invaluable for improving your own production skills.

For Music Educators

Stem separation is a powerful classroom tool. Isolating individual instruments makes it far easier to teach students to hear individual parts in a complex arrangement — demonstrating the bass line in a Steely Dan track, or the chord voicings of a Bill Evans piano recording, without the other instruments competing for attention.

Understanding Separation Quality: What Affects It?

Not all separations will be perfect. Here are the factors that affect quality:

Audio Quality of the Source

Higher bitrate = better results. A 320kbps MP3 will produce noticeably cleaner stems than a 128kbps file. Lossless formats (WAV, FLAC, AIFF) produce the best results.

Genre Complexity

  • Best results: Singer-songwriter acoustic, jazz duo, classical piano, classic rock
  • Good results: Modern pop, country, hip-hop, EDM, blues
  • Harder: Heavy metal with lots of distorted guitars (the distortion timbre overlaps with noise), extremely dense orchestral recordings

Instrument Frequency Overlap

Instruments that share frequency ranges are hardest to separate. A distorted electric guitar and a dense synthesizer pad that both occupy the 500Hz–4kHz midrange will "bleed" into each other. A clean bass guitar and a kick drum both below 200Hz similarly share frequency space.

Practical Uses for Musicians

  • Drummers: Solo the drums to study complex fills from professional recordings, or mute the drums to play along with the song and practice your timing against the band.
  • Vocalists: Isolate the vocals to hear the exact pitch and vocal inflections of the singer. Practice pitch matching and blend techniques.
  • Producers: Create high-quality bootleg remixes by sampling isolated hooks without background noise. Analyse the production decisions of mastered tracks.
  • Guitar teachers: Use isolated guitar stems to demonstrate exact techniques to students without the full-band mix distracting from the guitar part.
  • Music transcribers: Isolate any instrument to make transcription dramatically faster and more accurate.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Is Demucs stem separation completely free to use on Guitariz?

A: Yes, completely free. There are no track limits, no account registration requirements, and no duration caps. You can process as many tracks as you need.

Q: How long does the separation process take?

A: Processing time depends on the length and complexity of the audio file and current server load. A 3-minute song typically processes in 30-90 seconds for the 2-stem vocal model, and 60-180 seconds for the full 6-stem model.

Q: Does the audio quality of my stems depend on my internet connection?

A: No. Processing happens on our server. Once the stems are ready, they download to your device at maximum speed regardless of how long the processing took.

Q: Can I use separated stems commercially?

A: This depends entirely on the copyright status of the original audio. Using stems from commercially released music for your own private practice, learning, and transcription is generally covered by fair use principles. Using them in a publicly released remix or commercial sample requires the appropriate synchronization and master licenses from the copyright holders.

Q: Why does my vocal stem still have some faint instrumental bleed?

A: No stem separation is 100% perfect — some bleed (artifacts of other instruments heard faintly in the wrong stem) is normal. The amount of bleed varies significantly by song. Acoustic and folk recordings typically have very clean separations. Dense rock and EDM mixes may have more noticeable bleed in challenging frequency ranges.

Q: Can I separate stems from a YouTube video?

A: Upload the audio directly as an MP3 or WAV file. Download the audio from the YouTube video using any YouTube-to-MP3 converter, then upload it to the Stem Separator.

Q: What is the difference between the 2-stem and 6-stem models?

A: The 2-stem model separates audio into Vocals and Everything Else (instrumental). Because it only solves one separation problem, it can allocate the full capacity of the neural network to producing the cleanest possible vocal/instrumental split. The 6-stem model simultaneously separates Vocals, Drums, Bass, Guitar, Piano, and Other into 6 individual tracks. This is more complex and may produce slightly less clean individual stems compared to using the dedicated 2-stem model for vocals alone.

title: Introduction to Indian Ragas on Guitar
description: Master the sound of Indian Classical Music on the guitar. Learn the ten Thaats, Raga Bilawal, Raga Yaman, and how to configure scales.
author: Abhinav Vaidya
html:
Indian Classical Music is a rich, modal musical system that spans thousands of years. While Western music is heavily focused on chord progressions and harmony, Indian classical music focuses on melody and microtones.

Translating this sound to the guitar can open up new sonic palettes for your solos, fusion projects, and acoustic playing. In this comprehensive guide, we will break down the absolute basics of Indian Ragas on the guitar — from the solfege system and parent scales to practical playing techniques and specific Raga examples you can start playing today.

Why Ragas on Guitar?

The guitar is a Western instrument, but it is uniquely versatile. Its fretboard allows you to play scales in any key using the same shapes, and techniques like slides, bends, and hammer-ons mimic the vocal-like qualities that are central to Indian classical music.

Many fusion guitarists — including John McLaughlin, Shakti, and Prasanna — have explored the intersection of Western guitar technique and Indian classical theory. The result is a uniquely expressive musical vocabulary that combines the rhythmic drive of Western electric guitar with the meditative, melodic depth of Indian raga systems.

Whether you play acoustic fingerstyle, jazz, blues, or rock lead guitar, understanding Ragas will fundamentally change how you think about scales, melody, and improvisation.

1. The Concept of Swaras (Notes)

In Indian music, notes are called Swaras. Instead of C-D-E-F-G-A-B, the Indian solfege system (Sargam) uses:

  • Sa (Shadja) — The Tonic / Root note. Always fixed.
  • Re (Rishabha) — The Second
  • Ga (Gandhara) — The Third
  • Ma (Madhyama) — The Fourth
  • Pa (Panchama) — The Fifth. Always fixed (like Sa).
  • Dha (Dhaivata) — The Sixth
  • Ni (Nishada) — The Seventh

Unlike Western music, where the root note changes when you modulate keys, the note Sa is always your fixed root. You select a drone key (e.g., E), and all other notes are played relative to E.

Shuddha (Natural) and Vikrit (Altered) Notes

In Indian theory, the notes Re, Ga, Ma, Dha, and Ni each have two forms:

  • Shuddha — The natural, standard position
  • Komal (Vikrit flat) — Lowered by a half step (for Re, Ga, Dha, Ni)
  • Teevra (Vikrit sharp) — Raised by a half step (only for Ma)

This gives us 12 unique chromatic positions — the same 12 semitones as Western theory, but named and conceptualized differently.

Swara Shuddha Komal Western Equivalent (Sa=C)
Sa C — C
Re D Db (Komal Re) D / C#
Ga E Eb (Komal Ga) E / Eb
Ma F — F
Teevra Ma — F# (Teevra Ma) F#
Pa G — G
Dha A Ab (Komal Dha) A / Ab
Ni B Bb (Komal Ni) B / Bb

2. The 10 Thaats (Parent Scales)

In Hindustani classical music (the North Indian tradition), Ragas are categorized under 10 parent scales called Thaats. Think of these as the Indian equivalent to the 7 diatonic modes in Western music. Each Thaat uses exactly 7 notes and serves as a template from which dozens of specific Ragas are derived.

Here are the 10 Thaats with their Western equivalent scales:

Thaat Notes (Sa-fixed) Western Equivalent Character
Bilawal S R G M P D N Major / Ionian Bright, serene
Kalyan / Yaman S R G M# P D N Lydian Ethereal, uplifting
Khamaj S R G M P D n Mixolydian Playful, folksy
Bhairav S r G M P d N Persian / Double Harmonic Mysterious, spiritual
Poorvi S r G M# P d N — Complex, late evening
Marwa S r G M# P D N — Tense, late afternoon
Kafi S R g M P D n Dorian Introspective, blues-like
Asavari S R g M P d n Aeolian / Natural Minor Melancholic, feminine
Bhairavi S r g M P d n Phrygian Poignant, devotional
Todi S r g M# P d N — Complex, morning

(Uppercase = Shuddha; lowercase = Komal; M# = Teevra Ma)

Thaat Bilawal (The Major Scale)

This is identical to the Western Major scale (Ionian Mode). All notes are natural.

  • Sargam: Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni
  • Formula: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7

Thaat Yaman / Kalyan (The Lydian Mode)

This scale uses a sharp 4th note (Teevra Ma). It creates an ethereal, meditative sound — the sound of anticipation and longing. Many classical Indian movie songs are based in Yaman.

  • Sargam: Sa Re Ga Ma# Pa Dha Ni
  • Formula: 1 2 3 #4 5 6 7

Thaat Bhairav (Double Harmonic / Persian Scale)

One of the most distinctive Thaats — it uses Komal Re (b2) and Komal Dha (b6), creating the characteristic "exotic" sound associated with Indian and Middle Eastern music in Western ears. This scale is used for serious, spiritual, and devotional Ragas performed in the early morning.

  • Sargam: Sa Komal-Re Ga Ma Pa Komal-Dha Ni
  • Formula: 1 b2 3 4 5 b6 7

To visualize how these parent scales lay out across the guitar fretboard, check out our interactive Indian Raga Theory Lab, which maps all 10 Thaats onto a 24-fret interactive guitar neck.

3. Specific Ragas for Guitar: Three Examples

Raga Bhupali (Pentatonic Raga in Kalyan Thaat)

Raga Bhupali is one of the most beginner-friendly Ragas and an excellent starting point for Western guitarists. It is a pentatonic Raga — it uses only 5 of the 7 Swara positions.

  • Thaat: Kalyan
  • Notes: Sa Re Ga Pa Dha (skips Ma and Ni)
  • Western equivalent: Major Pentatonic scale
  • Time of day: Late evening / night
  • Mood (Rasa): Peaceful, romantic, longing

On guitar (with Sa = E):

Low to high: E - F# - G# - B - C#

This is identical to the E Major Pentatonic scale. Play it using standard pentatonic box shapes. To make it sound like Bhupali rather than rock pentatonic, you must follow the specific note-emphasis rules:

  • Vadi (most emphasized note): Ga (G#)
  • Samvadi (second most emphasized): Dha (C#)
  • Do NOT use the 4th (A) or 7th (D#) notes.
  • Play long, sustained notes on Ga and Dha. Ornament these notes heavily.

Raga Yaman (Full-Scale Raga)

Raga Yaman is based on Thaat Yaman (Lydian mode). It is one of the most commonly taught Ragas for beginners and is considered appropriate for evening performance.

  • Thaat: Kalyan (Yaman)
  • Notes: Sa Re Ga Ma# Pa Dha Ni (all 7 notes, with Teevra Ma)
  • Western equivalent: Lydian mode
  • Mood (Rasa): Serene beauty, longing, devotion

On guitar (with Sa = D):

D - E - F# - G# - A - B - C#

This is the D Lydian scale (same as A Major scale from the D root). The raised 4th note (G# in D Lydian) is the most distinctive characteristic — emphasize it in your phrases.

Key Yaman phrases on guitar:

  • The ascending phrase: Sa Re Ga, Ma# Ga Ma# Pa (D-E-F#, G#-F#-G#-A)
  • The characteristic descending ornament: Ni Dha Pa, Ma# Ga Re Sa

Raga Bageshri (Evening Raga in Kafi Thaat)

Raga Bageshri is based on Thaat Kafi (Dorian mode) and is associated with the late evening and rainy seasons. It has a deeply introspective, melancholic character.

  • Thaat: Kafi
  • Notes: Sa Re Komal-Ga Ma Pa Dha Komal-Ni
  • Western equivalent: Dorian mode
  • Mood (Rasa): Longing, nostalgia, the feeling of waiting

On guitar (with Sa = A):

A - B - C - D - E - F# - G

This is the A Dorian scale — the same notes as G Major, but starting from A. The characteristic phrase in Bageshri leaps between Komal Ga (C) and Ma (D), creating the distinctive yearning sound of this Raga.

4. Adapting Ragas on the Fretboard

Playing a Raga is more than just running up and down a scale. A Raga has specific rules that define its personality:

  • Arohana: The ascending path — the specific notes you are allowed to play going up.
  • Avarohana: The descending path — often different from the ascending path, using different notes.
  • Vadi: The most important, emphasized note in the Raga. This is the note you keep returning to.
  • Samvadi: The second most important note (usually a perfect fifth or fourth away from the Vadi).
  • Varjit Swara: Forbidden notes — notes that are completely excluded from a specific Raga even if they belong to the parent Thaat.
  • Gamak and Meend: Ornaments. Gamak is a fast, heavy oscillation. Meend is a smooth glissando slide between two notes.

For example, in Raga Bhupali, you are not allowed to play the 4th (Ma) or 7th (Ni) notes — they are Varjit (forbidden). The Arohana and Avarohana are identical: Sa - Re - Ga - Pa - Dha - Sa'.

5. Technique: How to Sound Like a Raga on Guitar

Western guitar technique and Indian classical ornament vocabulary overlap in surprising ways. Here are the key techniques to master:

Meend (Slide / Glissando)

Indian classical music is famous for smooth pitch slides between notes. On guitar, execute these as legato slides — pick the lower note and slide your fretting finger up or down to the target note without re-picking. Avoid the "bending blues style" bend and instead focus on smooth, even-speed glissandos across the full interval.

Gamak (Oscillation / Vibrato)

Gamak is a rapid, heavy oscillation on a single note. On guitar, this translates to wide vibrato — but the key difference from blues vibrato is that Gamak oscillates both above and below the target pitch, not just above. Try pushing the string up and then pulling it down in a rapid, even rhythm.

Kan Swara (Grace Note)

A Kan Swara is a brief ornamental touch on an adjacent note before the main note. On guitar, execute these as fast hammer-ons or pull-offs — a single grace note before the main note. These are used extensively to approach important notes like the Vadi.

Khatka (Short Ornament Burst)

A Khatka is a quick up-down-up oscillation across 2-3 notes. On guitar: from the target note, quickly hammer-on one note above, pull off back to the target, and hammer-on again. It sounds like: N-N+1-N in rapid succession.

6. Practical Exercise: Your First Raga Improvisation

Use this structured approach to play your first Raga-style improvisation on guitar:

  1. Set your drone: Use the drone feature in the Guitariz Jam Studio, set it to your Sa note (e.g., E), and let it ring continuously in the background. This gives your ear a fixed reference throughout the practice.

  2. Play Bhupali notes slowly: Using Sa = E, the notes are: E, F#, G#, B, C#. Play each note one at a time, very slowly. Let each note ring out. Notice how each note "feels" against the E drone.

  3. Apply Meend: Play E to F# using a slide. Play G# to B using a slide. Notice how the slides sound much more vocal and Indian than simply picking both notes separately.

  4. Emphasize the Vadi (G# in Bhupali): Return to G# frequently in your improvisation. Let it ring. Apply Gamak (vibrato) to it. This is the note the Raga "lives on."

  5. Explore both directions: Play ascending (E F# G# B C# E), then descending (E C# B G# F# E). Then mix them freely, being careful not to use A or D (the forbidden notes).

Explore the full fretboard mapping of 20+ common Hindustani and Carnatic scales using our free Raga Scale Explorer.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Do I need to know classical Indian music to play Ragas on guitar?

A: Not at all. Understanding the basic concepts of Swaras (notes), Thaats (parent scales), and Arohana/Avarohana (ascending/descending rules) is enough to begin exploring Raga-inspired improvisation on guitar. The deeper you go into the theory, the more authentically you can approach the style, but even a basic understanding opens up a rich new melodic vocabulary.

Q: What is the difference between Hindustani and Carnatic classical music?

A: Hindustani classical music is the North Indian tradition, while Carnatic classical music is the South Indian tradition. Both are ancient, sophisticated systems with overlapping but distinct Raga systems, rhythmic frameworks (Tala), and performance styles. The Thaats system described in this article belongs to the Hindustani tradition. Carnatic music uses a parallel system of 72 Melakarta parent scales.

Q: Can I use guitar bends to play microtones in Ragas?

A: Yes! Many Ragas involve andolan — a slow, gentle oscillation around a note that is slightly flatter or sharper than the equal-tempered Western pitch. Guitar bends are perfect for this. Raga Darbari Kanada, for example, uses a Komal Ga that is slightly flatter than the standard Eb — this microtonal inflection is what gives the Raga its distinctive character and is very achievable with a subtle bend on the guitar.

Q: What time of day should I practice specific Ragas?

A: In classical Indian performance tradition, Ragas are associated with specific times of day and seasons. Morning Ragas like Bhairav and Todi are meant to be performed at dawn. Evening Ragas like Yaman and Bhupali are meant for sunset and the early night. This association reflects the emotional and philosophical character of the Raga — you don't need to follow this strictly for practice, but it's a beautiful aspect of the tradition worth knowing.

Q: Is the guitar tuned differently for Indian classical music?

A: Most fusion guitarists keep standard EADGBE tuning. However, some players use open tunings where the open strings form a drone chord that provides a harmonic foundation. Open D tuning (DADF#AD) works well for Ragas based in D, as the open strings provide a Sa-Pa-Sa drone. Sitar players use a sympathetic string drone called a taraf — on guitar, you can simulate this by letting open strings ring sympathetically while you play.

title: How to Identify Chords by Ear for Guitarists
description: Master the art of transcribing music. Learn how to identify keys, recognize chord progressions, and figure out guitar chords by ear with active listening methods.
author: Abhinav Vaidya
html:
Have you ever listened to a song and wanted to play along instantly, but couldn't find the chords online? Or maybe the chords you found online just sounded... off?

Learning how to identify guitar chords by ear is one of the most liberating skills you can develop as a musician. It transforms you from someone who just reads tabs to someone who truly understands the music. A guitarist with a well-trained ear can walk into any jam session, hear a progression once, and immediately play along in the correct key.

In this guide, we'll break down the exact step-by-step process professionals use to transcribe chords by ear — from absolute beginners to advanced jazz players.

Why Ear Training Changes Everything

Many guitarists spend years reading tabs without ever developing their ear. This creates a frustrating limitation: you can only play what someone else has already written down for you.

Ear training breaks this ceiling. Once you can identify chords by ear, you can:

  • Learn any song in minutes, not days
  • Jam with other musicians in real time
  • Write your own chord progressions from scratch
  • Transpose songs to any key instantly
  • Catch wrong chords in tabs you find online

The good news: ear training is a learnable skill. Nobody is born with it. It develops through consistent, structured practice.

Step 1: Find the Key Center (The Root)

Before you try to guess any chord, you must find the key center of the song. The key center is the "home base" — the note where the song feels resolved and at rest.

How to do it:

  1. Hum along with the song until you find a single note that sounds like it fits over almost the entire song, especially at the very end of a chorus or verse.
  2. Pick up your guitar and find that note on the low E or A string.
  3. If that note is, say, G, then the song is likely in either G Major or G Minor.

Major vs. Minor

Once you have your root note, determine whether the overall mood of the song feels happy and bright (Major) or sad and dark (Minor). This is an emotional judgment — trust it.

  • Songs in Major keys: most pop, country, dance music
  • Songs in Minor keys: blues, heavy rock, ballads, emotional pop

Useful shortcut: the I-IV-V

In virtually every genre of popular music, the most common chord movements are built on just three chords: the I (home), the IV (the chord a perfect fourth above), and the V (the chord a perfect fifth above). In G Major, these are G, C, and D. Learn these three chords in every key and you can play along with a huge proportion of all popular music.

Step 2: Listen to the Bassline

The secret weapon of transcribing chords is the bass player. In 90% of popular music, the bass guitar plays the root note of the active chord on the first beat of each measure.

If you can hear the bassline, you can figure out the chord progression:

  • Use high-quality headphones — open-back studio headphones like the Audio-Technica ATH-M50x give you much better low-frequency resolution than earbuds.
  • If you are struggling to hear the bass against the kick drum, try using our Stem Separator AI to isolate the bass track entirely, removing drums, vocals, and guitars so you can hear the bass line in complete clarity.
  • Match the bass notes to the notes on your guitar neck. If the bass plays C → G → A → F, those are the root notes of your chords!

Counting Beats

Get in the habit of counting beats while you listen. Mark the moment where the bass note changes. Most chord changes happen on beat 1 of a new bar. Once you identify the root note changes at each chord, you have the skeleton of your chord progression.

Step 3: Determine Chord Quality (Major vs. Minor)

Once you know the root notes (e.g., C, G, A, F), you need to determine if each chord is Major (happy, bright) or Minor (sad, dark).

The Simple Test:

Play the major version of the chord. If it sounds correct, you're good. If it sounds clashy or tense, try playing the minor version.

Root Try First Try Second
C C Major (C-E-G) C Minor (C-Eb-G)
G G Major (G-B-D) G Minor (G-Bb-D)
A A Major (A-C#-E) A Minor (A-C-E)
F F Major (F-A-C) F Minor (F-Ab-C)

Tip: If you're stuck, you can also run the song through our Chord AI Free Engine to get a visual map of the exact chord voicings in real-time as a reference checkpoint.

Step 4: Use the Roman Numeral System (Music Theory)

Music theory isn't just academic — it's a shortcut. In any given key, only certain chords naturally occur.

For example, in a Major Key, the naturally occurring chords (diatonic chords) follow this pattern:

  • I (Major) — The home chord
  • ii (Minor) — Sounds introspective, frequently moves to V
  • iii (Minor) — Rarely used as a root position chord; usually decorative
  • IV (Major) — The "lift" chord; creates anticipation
  • V (Major) — Creates the most tension; wants to resolve to I
  • vi (Minor) — The relative minor; the most emotional chord in the key
  • vii° (Diminished) — Very tense; rarely heard in pop music

If the song is in G Major, the common chords you will encounter are:

  • G Major (I)
  • A Minor (ii)
  • B Minor (iii)
  • C Major (IV)
  • D Major (V)
  • E Minor (vi)

If you already identified the key as G Major, and you hear a chord with an E root, you can almost guarantee it's an E minor (vi) chord!

The Most Common Progressions in Pop Music

Over 50% of all pop songs use one of just a handful of chord progressions:

  1. I – V – vi – IV (C – G – Am – F in C Major) — "Let It Be," "No Woman No Cry," hundreds of others
  2. I – IV – V (C – F – G in C Major) — The foundational blues progression
  3. ii – V – I (Dm – G – C in C Major) — The backbone of all jazz harmony
  4. vi – IV – I – V (Am – F – C – G in C Major) — Anthemic pop and rock ballads

Learn to recognize these by ear and you will instantly be able to identify the progressions of an enormous number of songs.

Step 5: Identify 7th Chords and Extensions

Once you can reliably identify triads (major, minor, diminished), the next level is recognizing 7th chords.

The Four Main 7th Chord Sounds:

Major 7th (Maj7): Adds the major 7th note to a major triad. Creates a dreamy, lush, "floating" sound. Commonly used in jazz, bossa nova, and neo-soul. Example: Cmaj7 (C-E-G-B).

Dominant 7th (7): Adds the minor 7th note to a major triad. Creates a bluesy, tense sound that strongly wants to resolve to the I chord. This is the classic blues chord. Example: C7 (C-E-G-Bb).

Minor 7th (m7): Adds the minor 7th note to a minor triad. Creates a mellow, sophisticated, slightly sad sound. The bread-and-butter of smooth R&B and jazz. Example: Cm7 (C-Eb-G-Bb).

Half-Diminished (m7b5): Adds the minor 7th to a diminished triad. Creates a dark, tense, mysterious sound used in jazz and film scores. Example: Cm7b5 (C-Eb-Gb-Bb).

To practice recognizing 7th chords, use the Ear Training Arcade — specifically the Chord Recognition game, which plays random chord voicings for you to identify.

Step 6: Slow Down Difficult Sections

If a song is too fast to transcribe in real time, slow it down. Modern audio players and tools can reduce the tempo of a song by 50% or more without changing the pitch. This gives your ears and fingers time to keep up.

Tools for slowing down:

  • Audacity (free desktop app): Use "Change Tempo" effect to slow down without pitch shift
  • YouTube: Use the playback speed settings (⚙️ icon) to set speed to 0.75x or 0.5x
  • Guitariz BPM Detector: Upload a file to detect the original tempo before you start slowing it down — this gives you a reference for re-syncing later

Step 7: Use Technology as a Feedback Tool (Not a Crutch)

AI chord detection tools are an excellent way to verify your ear training, not replace it. Here is the ideal workflow:

  1. Listen and transcribe yourself first — spend 10-15 minutes trying to work out the chords purely by ear before looking up anything.
  2. Check against an AI tool — run the song through Guitariz Chord AI and compare its output to what you heard.
  3. Analyse discrepancies — where you were wrong, listen again carefully to that specific section. Understanding why you misidentified a chord is the core learning moment.

This feedback loop is far more effective than simply reading tabs and produces faster improvement than ear training exercises in isolation.

Practice Routine for Beginners

If you are just starting, use this 4-week plan:

Week 1: Major vs. Minor

  • Pick 10 random songs this week
  • For each song, determine: Is it in a Major or Minor key?
  • Just this one binary decision trains your ear enormously

Week 2: Identify the I–IV–V

  • Pick simple country, folk, or blues songs (3-chord songs)
  • Identify the three main chords and their Roman numerals
  • Songs to try: "Knockin' on Heaven's Door," "Sweet Home Chicago"

Week 3: Find the vi Chord

  • Add the vi (relative minor) chord to your recognition toolkit
  • Listen for the emotional "drop" feeling when a song moves from I to vi
  • Songs to try: "Let Her Go" by Passenger, "Stand By Me"

Week 4: Transcribe a Full Progression

  • Pick a song you love and attempt to transcribe the entire chord progression
  • Verify with a chord AI tool and analyze any errors

Summary Checklist to Practice

Next time you try to learn a song, turn off the internet tab search and follow this loop:

  1. Hum the root note to find the key.
  2. Listen to the low frequencies for the bass progression.
  3. Analyze the mood (Major or Minor?).
  4. Use theory (like the Circle of Fifths) to predict what chords should come next.
  5. Verify with AI if you get stuck — then analyze the discrepancies.

Like any physical muscle, ear training takes consistency. Start with simple 3-chord pop and folk songs, and gradually work your way up to complex jazz or rock progressions. With dedicated daily practice of even just 10-15 minutes, most musicians notice a significant improvement in their transcription speed within 4-6 weeks.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How long does it take to learn to identify chords by ear?

A: Most guitarists can identify basic major and minor triads after 4-8 weeks of daily 15-minute practice sessions. Identifying 7th chords and complex extensions typically takes 3-6 months. Perfect pitch (identifying notes without a reference) takes years and is not required for most practical music applications.

Q: Is relative pitch or perfect pitch more useful for a guitarist?

A: Relative pitch is far more practical and useful for 99% of guitarists. Relative pitch means you can identify intervals and chords when you have a reference note. Perfect pitch (identifying notes with no reference) is a rare gift that is hard to train in adults, and most professional session guitarists and composers use relative pitch exclusively.

Q: What is the best song to start ear training with?

A: Start with songs that use only 3 chords in a major key. "Knockin' on Heaven's Door" (G, D, Am/C), "La Bamba" (C, F, G), and "Sweet Home Chicago" (E, A, B blues) are classic starter tracks. They have clear harmonic motion, steady tempos, and minimal studio production that might confuse your ear.

Q: Should I use headphones or speakers for ear training?

A: High-quality headphones are generally better because they give you a clearer, more separated stereo image. Studio-grade closed-back headphones (like the Audio-Technica ATH-M50x) are ideal because they isolate external noise and give you flat, accurate frequency response. Avoid bass-boosted consumer headphones which can make the low end muddy and harder to hear the bass notes clearly.

Q: Why does a chord I identified sound "almost right" but slightly off?

A: This usually means you have the correct root note and chord quality (major/minor) but are missing an extension. The chord might be a 7th, sus2, or add9 variant. Try adding the 7th or 9th to the chord and see if it clicks. Alternatively, it could be a chord inversion — the same notes, but with a different note in the bass.
